    Boundaries

    boundaries.Rmd

    A boundary says what a map is about: it draws the area’s outline, frames the view around it, and switches on the vignette that dims everything else. Without one, the map simply fits the data:

    library(quickmap)                          # load the quickmap library
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs = "Wandsworth"                  # the boundary to draw
)

    1. One, several, or all 

    quickmap(
  from_rdata("sensors_london.RData", "no2",
             name = "Sensors"),
  boroughs = c("Merton", "Wandsworth")     # NEW: two boundaries
)

    boroughs = "All" draws every London borough. Minor misspellings of common names are corrected automatically; an unrecognised name lists the valid ones.

    2. Write the names on the map

    On a multi-area map, label the areas themselves:

    quickmap(
  from_rdata("sensors_london.RData", "no2",
             name = "Sensors"),
  boroughs = c("Merton", "Wandsworth"),
  boundary_labels = TRUE                   # NEW: area names on the map
)

    3. The vignette

    With a boundary drawn, everything outside it is dimmed by default, so the reader’s eye goes to the area in question. vignette = FALSE shows the surroundings at full brightness; the dimming colour follows the map’s theme (Styling and themes).

    quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs = "Wandsworth",
  vignette = FALSE                         # NEW: no dimming outside
)

    4. No boundary at all

    Leave boroughs out and no outline is drawn, no vignette applies, and the view fits the data — right for data that isn’t about one administrative area:

    quickmap("tubes_wandsworth.csv")   # data-only map

    See also

    • Get started steps 3–4 — boundaries in the build-up.
    • Ward-level boundaries and finer-grained labelling are on the roadmap (pre-v1.0 defect list) — this page will grow with them.
    • ?quickmap — boroughs, boundary_labels, vignette.
